title: Count the bins
prompt:
Before drawing a histogram, count it. Finish `count_bins(costs, width)` so it returns a dictionary from each bin's starting value to how many costs fall in that bin. A cost of 42 with width 40 goes in the bin that starts at 40.

When it works, `python3 bins.py` prints the counts for the twelve fictional tickets.
hints: `cost // width` says how many whole widths fit below the cost. Multiply it by `width` again to get the bin's start.
Use `counts.get(start, 0) + 1` so a bin you have not seen yet starts at zero.
Inside the loop: `start = cost // width * width`, then `counts[start] = counts.get(start, 0) + 1`. Return `dict(sorted(counts.items()))` so the bins come out in order.
explain_after: Matplotlib's `hist` draws exactly this kind of count as bars [ml-102]. In the book, `b03_hist` asks Matplotlib for the same bins and gets the same counts you just made by hand.
